title: Bivariate Viz — Exercises
text:
Exercise 3: Reflect
Summarize the relationship between the Republican support in 2020 and 2016. Be sure to comment on:

the strength of the relationship: weak/moderate/strong
the direction of the relationship: positive/negative
outliers, ie, in what state do counties deviate from the national trend? Any ideas why this might be the case?

There is a strong, positive, approximately linear relationship between Republican support in 2016 and Republican support in 2020. Counties with higher Republican support in 2016 generally also had higher Republican support in 2020. Most counties follow the national trend closely, although some counties deviate from it. Utah is especially notable because the 2016 election was unusual there: independent candidate Evan McMullin received substantial support, which reduced the Republican percentage compared with what we might otherwise expect.

title: Bivariate Viz — Exercises
text:
Exercise 4: Visualizing Trend
The trend of the relationship between repub_pct_20 and repub_pct_16 is clearly positive and (mostly) linear. We can highlight this trend by adding a model “smooth” to the plot:

Codeggplot(elections, aes(y = repub_pct_20, x = repub_pct_16)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth()







Part a
Construct a new plot that contains the model smooth but does not include the individual point glyphs.

Codeggplot(elections, aes(y = repub_pct_20, x = repub_pct_16)) +
  geom_smooth()







Part b
By default, geom_smooth() adds a smooth, localized model line. To examine the “best” linear model, we can specify method = "lm". It’s pretty similar in this example.

Codeggplot(elections, aes(y = repub_pct_20, x = repub_pct_16)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm")

title: Bivariate Viz — Exercises
text:
Exercise 5: Your Turn
To examine how the 2020 results are related to some county demographics, construct scatterplots of repub_pct_20 vs median_rent, and repub_pct_20 vs median_age. Summarize the relationship between these two variables and comment on which is the better predictor of repub_pct_20, median_rent or median_age.

Code# Scatterplot of repub_pct_20 vs median_rent


ggplot(elections, aes(x = median_rent, y = repub_pct_20)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth()








Code# Scatterplot of repub_pct_20 vs median_age

ggplot(elections, aes(x = median_age, y = repub_pct_20)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth()







The plots let us compare how strongly each demographic variable is associated with Republican support. The better predictor is the variable whose scatterplot shows a clearer and tighter pattern with repub_pct_20, with less scatter around the overall trend.

title: Bivariate Viz — Exercises
text:
Exercise 6: A Sad Scatterplot
Next, let’s explore the relationship between a county’s 2020 Republican support repub_pct_20 and the historical political trends in its state. In this case repub_pct_20 is quantitative, but historical is categorical. Explain why a scatterplot might not be an effective visualization for exploring this relationship. (What questions does / doesn’t it help answer?)

Codeggplot(elections, aes(y = repub_pct_20, x = historical)) +
  geom_point()







scatterplot is not very effective because historical is categorical, so all counties are stacked into only three x-axis positions. This creates a lot of overlapping points and makes it difficult to see the distribution, center, and variability of Republican support within each category. A boxplot, violin plot, or density plot makes those differences much easier to compare.

title: Bivariate Viz — Exercises
section: Exercise 7: Quantitative vs Categorical: Violins & Boxes
text:
Exercise 7: Quantitative vs Categorical: Violins & Boxes
Though the above scatterplot did group the counties by historical category, it’s nearly impossible to pick out meaningful patterns in 2020 Republican support in each category. Let’s try adding 2 different geom layers to the frame:

Code# Side-by-side violin plots
ggplot(elections, aes(y = repub_pct_20, x = historical)) +
  geom_violin()








Code# Side-by-side boxplots (defined below)
ggplot(elections, aes(y = repub_pct_20, x = historical)) +
  geom_boxplot()







Box plots are constructed from five numbers: the minimum, 25th percentile, median, 75th percentile, and maximum value of a quantitative variable:

REFLECT:
Summarize what you’ve learned about the 2020 Republican county-level support within and between red/purple/blue states.
There is a fairly large range of Republican support within blue, purple, and red states, so counties within the same type of state can still differ substantially. However, Republican county-level support tends to be higher in historically red states, lower in historically blue states, and intermediate in purple states. There is still considerable overlap among the three groups.

section: Exercise 8: Quantitative vs Categorical: Intuition Check
text:
Exercise 8: Quantitative vs Categorical: Intuition Check






ImportantBe Quick



Don’t spend more than 3 minutes on this!


We can also visualize the relationship between repub_pct_20 and historical using our familiar density plots. In the plot below, notice that we simply created a separate density plot for each historical category. The plot itself is “bad” but we’ll fix it below. Try to adjust the code chunk below, which starts with a density plot of repub_pct_20 alone, to re-create this image.

title: Bivariate Viz — Exercises
section: Exercise 9: Quantitative vs Categorical: Density Plots
text:
Exercise 9: Quantitative vs Categorical: Density Plots
Work through the chunks below and address the comments therein.

Code# Name two "bad" things about this plot
ggplot(elections, aes(x = repub_pct_20, fill = historical)) +
  geom_density()







The bad things about the gragh is the fact that I can’t fully see the purple and blue graph since it is overlay by the the red state as it covers half of the other two graph. Moreover, the color of the gragh is not corresponding with the actual value color itself

Code# What does scale_fill_manual do?
ggplot(elections, aes(x = repub_pct_20, fill = historical)) +
  geom_density() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("blue", "purple", "red"))







scale_fill_manual() munually pick the color for the graph but not letting R to pick it automaticlly

Code# What does alpha = 0.5 do?
# Play around with different values of alpha, between 0 and 1
ggplot(elections, aes(x = repub_pct_20, fill = historical)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.5) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("blue", "purple", "red"))







alpha = 0 means completely transparent, while alpha = 1 means completely opaque. alpha = 0.5 makes the densities partially transparent so overlapping distributions are easier to see.

Code# What does facet_wrap do?!
ggplot(elections, aes(x = repub_pct_20, fill = historical)) +
  geom_density() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("blue", "purple", "red")) +
  facet_wrap(~historical)







It creates a separate small plot for each historical category instead of putting all three distributions on one graph.

Code# Let's try a similar grouping strategy with a histogram instead of density plot.
# Why is this terrible?
ggplot(elections, aes(x = repub_pct_20, fill = historical)) +
  geom_histogram(color = "white") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("blue", "purple", "red"))







The three histograms are overlapping, making it difficult to see and compare the actual distributions of Republican support among the historical categories. Differences in the number of counties in each category also make the heights difficult to compare directly. ## Exercise 10: Reflect
We’ve now learned 3 (of many) ways to visualize the relationship between a quantitative and categorical variable: side-by-side violins, boxplots, and density plots.

Which do you like best? I personally prefer the boxplot the best which help me to visualize the data the best without overlapping
What is one pro of density plots relative to boxplots?One advantage of a density plot is that it shows the full shape of the distribution instead of reducing the data to only a few summary statistics
What is one con of density plots relative to boxplots? One disadvantage is that density plots can be harder to interpret and compare precisely than boxplots.

title: Bivariate Viz — Exercises
text:
Exercise 12: Categorical vs Categorical
Construct the following 4 bar plot visualizations.

Code# A stacked bar plot
# How are the "historical" and "winner_20" variables mapped to the plot, i.e. what roles do they play?
ggplot(elections, aes(x = historical, fill = winner_20)) +
  geom_bar()







historical determines the categories on the x-axis, while winner_20 determines the fill color inside each bar.

Code# A faceted bar plot
ggplot(elections, aes(x = winner_20)) +
  geom_bar() +
  facet_wrap(~historical)








Code# A side-by-side bar plot
# Note the new argument to geom_bar
ggplot(elections, aes(x = historical, fill = winner_20)) +
  geom_bar(position = "dodge")








Code# A proportional bar plot
# Note the new argument to geom_bar
ggplot(elections, aes(x = historical, fill = winner_20)) +
  geom_bar(position = "fill")







Part a
Name one pro and one con of using the “proportional bar plot” instead of one of the other three options.
Pro: A proportional bar plot makes it easier to compare the percentage of Democratic and Republican county wins between red, purple, and blue states even when the groups contain different numbers of counties. Con: It hides the actual number of counties in each group because every bar is forced to have the same height.
Part b
What’s your favorite bar plot from part and why?
I prefer the proportional bar plot because it makes it easiest to compare the proportions of Democratic and Republican county wins across historically blue, purple, and red states. Since every bar has the same total height, differences in the total number of counties do not distract from the comparison of proportions.

title: Bivariate Viz — Exercises
text:
Exercise 14: State Support (Optional)
The above visualizations are foundational and important. But they’re not the only way to visualize the variables in our dataset.
Suppose we wanted to better understand how the 2020 Republican support varied from county to county within each state. Since repub_pct_20 is quantitative and state_abbr is categorical, we could make a density plot of repub_pct_20 for each state. Reflect on why this is bad.
With about 50 states, the density curves overlap heavily and the legend becomes difficult to use, so individual state distributions are hard to distinguish.

Codeggplot(elections, aes(x = repub_pct_20, fill = state_abbr)) + 
  geom_density(alpha = 0.5)







A facet wrap would also be bad!

Codeggplot(elections, aes(x = repub_pct_20)) + 
  geom_density(alpha = 0.5) + 
  facet_wrap(~ state_abbr)







When we want to compare the distribution of some quantitative outcome among many groups / categories, a ridgeline plot can be a good option. These are also called joy plots, named after the album cover for “Unknown Pleasures” by Joy Division. (Look it up!) To make a ridgeline plot, we can use the geom_density_ridges() function from the ggridges package.

Code# Remember to install ggridges package before calling it
library(ggridges)

# Make our first joy plot
# THINK: What DON'T you like about this?
ggplot(elections, aes(x = repub_pct_20, y = state_abbr)) + 
  geom_density_ridges()








Code# Let's put the states in order by Republican support, not alphabet
# How do you think fct_reorder works? We'll learn about this later in the semester.
ggplot(elections, aes(x = repub_pct_20, y = fct_reorder(state_abbr, repub_pct_20))) + 
  geom_density_ridges(alpha = 0.5)








Code# YOUR TURN: color/fill the ridges according to a state's historical voting patterns 
# and add meaningful axis labels
ggplot(
  elections,
  aes(
    x = repub_pct_20,
    y = fct_reorder(state_abbr, repub_pct_20),
    fill = historical
  )
) +
  geom_density_ridges(alpha = 0.5) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("blue", "purple", "red")) +
  labs(
    x = "Republican Support in 2020",
    y = "State",
    fill = "Historical Voting Pattern"
  )







Follow-up questions

Which states tend to have the most variability in outcomes from county to county? The least?
What other interesting patterns do you notice?
Does this plot prompt any other questions?

title: Spatial Viz
text:
Preview
You’ll explore some R spatial viz tools below. In general, there are two important pieces to every map:
Piece 1: A dataset
This dataset must include either:
Piece 2: A background map
We need latitude and longitude coordinates to specify the boundaries for your regions of interest (eg: countries, states). This is where it gets really sticky!
In short, the code for spatial viz gets very specialized. The goal of these exercises is to:
You can skip around as you wish and it’s totally fine if you don’t finish everything. Just come back at some point to play around.

title: Spatial Viz
text:
location coordinates for your points of interest (for point maps); or
variable outcomes for your regions of interest (for choropleth maps)




County-level, state-level, country-level, continent-level info live in multiple places.
Where we grab this info can depend upon whether we want to make a point map or a choropleth map. (The background maps can be used somewhat interchangeably, but it requires extra code :/)
Where we grab this info can also depend upon the structure of our data and how much data wrangling / cleaning we’re up for. For choropleth maps, the labels of regions in our data must match those in the background map. For example, if our data labels states with their abbreviations (eg: MN) and the background map refers to them as full names in lower case (eg: minnesota), we have to wrangle our data so that it matches the background map.



play around and experience the wide variety of spatial viz tools out there
understand the difference between point maps and choropleth maps
have fun

title: Spatial Viz
text:
Interactive Points with leaflet

Leaflet is an open-source JavaScript library for creating maps. We can use it inside R through the leaflet package.
This uses a different plotting framework than ggplot2, but still has a tidyverse feel (which will become more clear as we learn other tidyverse tools!).
The general steps are as follows:

Create a map widget by calling leaflet() and telling it the data to use.
Add a base map using addTiles() (the default) or addProviderTiles().
Add layers to the map using layer functions (e.g. addMarkers(), addPolygons()).
Print the map widget to display it.

✏️ Map Points with Leaflet
Earlier this semester, I asked for the latitude and longitude of one of your favorite places. I rounded these to the nearest whole number, so that they’re near to but not exactly at those places. Let’s load the data and map it!

Codefave_places <- read.csv("https://hash-mac.github.io/ds112site-f26/data/our_fave_places.csv")

# Check it out
head(fave_places)




  latitude  longitude
1 48.65023 -123.39852
2 54.99000   -7.32000
3 45.00767  -93.16915
4 49.86262  -97.13224
5 44.93807  -93.16851
6 44.97372   93.22742


You can use a “two-finger scroll” to zoom in and out.

Code# Load the leaflet package
library(leaflet)



Code# Just a plotting frame
leaflet(data = fave_places)






Code# Now what do we have?
leaflet(data = fave_places) |> 
  addTiles()






Code# Now what do we have?
# longitude and latitude refer to the variables in our data
leaflet(data = fave_places) |> 
  addTiles() |> 
  addMarkers(lng = ~longitude, lat = ~latitude)






Code# Since we named them "longitude" and "latitude", the function
# automatically recognizes these variables. No need to write them!
leaflet(data = fave_places) |> 
  addTiles() |> 
  addMarkers()





✏️ Explore Zoom Limits
PLAY AROUND! This map is interactive. Zoom in on one location. Keep zooming – what level of detail can you get into? How does that detail depend upon where you try to zoom in (thus what are the limitations of this tool)?
✏️ Customize Details
We can change all sorts of details in leaflet maps.

Code# Load package needed to change color
library(gplots)

# We can add colored circles instead of markers at each location
leaflet(data = fave_places) |> 
  addTiles() |> 
  addCircles(color = "red")






Code# We can change the background
# Mark locations with yellow dots
# And connect the dots, in their order in the dataset, with green lines
# (These green lines don't mean anything here, but would if this were somebody's travel path!)
leaflet(data = fave_places) |>
  addProviderTiles("USGS") |>
  addCircles(weight = 10, opacity = 1, color = "yellow") |>
  addPolylines(
    lng = ~longitude,
    lat = ~latitude,
    color = "green"
  )





In general:

addProviderTiles() changes the base map.
To explore all available provider base maps, type providers in the console. (Though some don’t work :/)

Use addMarkers() or addCircles() to mark locations. Type ?addControl into the console to pull up a help file which summarizes the aesthetics of these markers and how you can change them. For example:


weight = how thick to make the lines, points, pixels

opacity = transparency (like alpha in ggplot2)


✏️ Map Starbucks Locations
The starbucks data, compiled by Danny Kaplan, contains information about every Starbucks in the world at the time the data were collected, including Latitude and Longitude:

Code# Import starbucks location data
starbucks <- read.csv("https://mac-stat.github.io/data/starbucks.csv")


Let’s focus on only those in Minnesota for now:

Code# Don't worry about the syntax
starbucks_mn <- starbucks %>% 
  dplyr::filter(
    dplyr::pick(8) == "US",  # 8th column is Country
    dplyr::pick(7) == "MN"   # 7th column is State/Province
  )


Create a leaflet map of the Starbucks locations in Minnesota. Keep it simple – go back to ✏️ Map Points with Leaflet for an example.

title: Spatial Viz
text:
Static Points
Leaflet is very powerful and fun. But:

It’s not great when we have lots of points to map – it takes lots of time.
It makes good interactive maps, but we often need a static map (eg: we can not print interactive maps!).

Let’s explore how to make point maps with ggplot(), not leaflet().
✏️ Plot Simple Scatterplot
Let’s start with the ggplot() tools we already know. Construct a scatterplot of all starbucks locations, not just those in Minnesota, with:

Latitude and Longitude coordinates (which goes on the y-axis?!)
Make the points transparent (alpha = 0.2) and smaller (size = 0.2)

It’s pretty cool that the plots we already know can provide some spatial context. But what don’t you like about this plot?

Codelibrary(ggplot2)
ggplot(starbucks, aes(x = Longitude, y = Latitude)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.2, size = 0.2)







✏️ Add Country Background
Let’s add a background map of country-level boundaries.
First, we can grab country-level boundaries from the rnaturalearth package.

Code# Load the package
library(rnaturalearth)

# Get info about country boundaries across the world
# in a "sf" or simple feature format
world_boundaries <- ne_countries(returnclass = "sf")


In your console, type world_boundaries to check out what’s stored there. Don’t print it our in your Rmd – printing it would be really messy there (even just the head()).
Run the chunks below to build up a new map.

Code# What does this code produce?
# What geom are we using for the point map?
ggplot(world_boundaries) + 
  geom_sf()








Code# Load package needed to change map theme
library(mosaic)

# Add a point for each Starbucks
# NOTE: The Starbucks info is in our starbucks data, not world_boundaries
# How does this change how we use geom_point?!
ggplot(world_boundaries) + 
  geom_sf() + 
  geom_point(
    data = starbucks,
    aes(x = Longitude, y = Latitude),
    alpha = 0.3, size = 0.2, color = "darkgreen"
  ) +
  theme_map()







✏️ Summarize Starbucks Map
Summarize what you learned about Starbucks from this map.
✏️ Zoom into Countries
Instead of world_boundaries <- ne_countries(returnclass = 'sf') we could zoom in on…

the continent of Africa: ne_countries(continent = 'Africa', returnclass = 'sf')

a set of countries: ne_countries(country = c('france', 'united kingdom', 'germany'), returnclass = 'sf')

boundaries within a country: ne_states(country = 'united states of america', returnclass = 'sf')


Our goal here will be to map the Starbucks locations in Canada, Mexico, and the US.
To make this map, we again need two pieces of information.

Data on Starbucks for only Canada, Mexico, and the US, labeled as “CA”, “MX”, “US” in the starbucks data.


Code# We'll learn this syntax soon! Don't worry about it now.
starbucks_cma <- starbucks |> 
  filter(Country %in% c('CA', 'MX', 'US'))



A background map ofYes state- and national-level boundaries in Canada, Mexico, and the US. This requires ne_states() in the rnaturalearth package where the countries are labeled ‘canada’, ‘mexico’, ‘united states of america’.


Codecma_boundaries <- ne_states(
  country = c("canada", "mexico", "united states of america"),
  returnclass = "sf")


Make the map!

Code# Just the boundaries
ggplot(cma_boundaries) + 
  geom_sf()








Code# Add the points
# And zoom in
ggplot(cma_boundaries) + 
  geom_sf() + 
  geom_point(
    data = starbucks_cma,
    aes(x = Longitude, y = Latitude),
    alpha = 0.3,
    size = 0.2,
    color = "darkgreen"
  ) +
  coord_sf(xlim = c(-179.14, -50)) +
  theme_map()







✏️ Map States & Counties
Let’s get an even higher resolution map of Starbucks locations within the states of Minnesota, Wisconsin, North Dakota, and South Dakota, with a background map at the county-level.
To make this map, we again need two pieces of information.

Data on Starbucks for only the states of interest.


Codestarbucks_midwest <- starbucks |> 
  filter(State.Province %in% c("MN", "ND", "SD", "WI"))



A background map of state- and county-level boundaries in these states. This requires st_as_sf() in the sf package, and map() in the maps package, where the countries are labeled ‘minnesota’, ‘north dakota’, etc.


Code# Load packages
library(sf)
library(maps)

# Get the boundaries
midwest_boundaries <- st_as_sf(
  maps::map("county",
            region = c("minnesota", "wisconsin", "north dakota", "south dakota"), 
            fill = TRUE, plot = FALSE))

# Check it out
head(midwest_boundaries)

Adjust the code below to make the plot! Remove the # to run it.

Codeggplot(midwest_boundaries) + 
  geom_sf() + 
  geom_point(
    data = starbucks_midwest,
    aes(x = Longitude, y = Latitude),
    alpha = 0.7,
    size = 0.2, 
    color = "darkgreen"
  ) + 
  theme_map()







✏️ Build Contour Maps
Especially when there are lots of point locations, and those locations start overlapping on a map, it can be tough to visualize areas of higher density. Consider the Starbucks locations in Canada, Mexico, and the US that we mapped earlier:

Code# Point map (we made this earlier)
ggplot(cma_boundaries) + 
  geom_sf() + 
  geom_point(
    data = starbucks_cma,
    aes(x = Longitude, y = Latitude),
    alpha = 0.3,
    size = 0.2,
    color = "darkgreen"
  ) +
  coord_sf(xlim = c(-179.14, -50), ylim = c(14.54, 83.11)) +
  theme_map()







Now check out the contour map.

Code# What changed in the plot?
# What changed in our code?!
ggplot(cma_boundaries) + 
  geom_sf() + 
  geom_density_2d(
    data = starbucks_cma,
    aes(x = Longitude, y = Latitude),
    size = 0.2,
    color = "darkgreen"
  ) +

title: Spatial Viz
text:
Choropleth Maps
Spatial data isn’t always in the form of point locations! For example, recall the state and county-level data on presidential elections.

Codeelections_by_state <-  read.csv("https://mac-stat.github.io/data/election_2020_by_state.csv")
elections_by_counties <- read.csv("https://mac-stat.github.io/data/election_2020_county.csv")


In these datasets, we’re interested in the overall election outcome by region (state or county), not the specific geographic location of some observation. Let’s wrangle our data first. We’ll focus on just a few variables of interest, and create a new variable (repub_20_categories) that discretizes the repub_pct_20 variable into increments of 5 percentage points (for states) or 10 percentage points (for counties):

Code# Don't worry about the code!

elections_by_state <- elections_by_state |> 
  filter(state_abbr != "DC") |> 
  select(state_name, state_abbr, repub_pct_20) |> 
  mutate(repub_20_categories = 
           cut(repub_pct_20, 
               breaks = seq(30, 70, by = 5), 
               labels = c("30-34", "35-39", "40-44", "45-49",
                          "50-54", "55-59", "60-64", "65-70"), 
               include.lowest = TRUE))

elections_by_counties <- elections_by_counties |> 
  select(state_name, state_abbr, county_name, county_fips,
          repub_pct_20, median_age, median_rent) |> 
  mutate(repub_20_categories = 
           cut(repub_pct_20, 
               breaks = seq(0, 100, by = 10),
               labels = c("0-9", "10-19", "20-29", "30-39", "40-49",
                          "50-59", "60-69", "70-79", "80-89", "90-100"),
               include.lowest = TRUE))


✏️ Map States with Choropleth
Let’s map the 2020 Republican support in each state, repub_pct_20.
We again need two pieces of information.

Data on elections in each state, which we already have: elections_by_state.
A background map of state boundaries in the US. The boundaries we used for point maps don’t work here. (Optional detail: they’re sf objects and we now need a data.frame object.) Instead, we can use the map_data() function from the ggplot2 package:


Code# Get the latitude and longitude coordinates of state boundaries
states_map <- map_data("state")

# Check it out
head(states_map)

       long      lat group order  region subregion
1 -87.46201 30.38968     1     1 alabama      <NA>
2 -87.48493 30.37249     1     2 alabama      <NA>
3 -87.52503 30.37249     1     3 alabama      <NA>
4 -87.53076 30.33239     1     4 alabama      <NA>
5 -87.57087 30.32665     1     5 alabama      <NA>
6 -87.58806 30.32665     1     6 alabama      <NA>


Important detail: Note that the region variable in states_map, and the state_name variable in elections_by_state both label states by the full name in lower case letters. This is critical to the background map and our data being able to communicate.

Codehead(states_map)

       long      lat group order  region subregion
1 -87.46201 30.38968     1     1 alabama      <NA>
2 -87.48493 30.37249     1     2 alabama      <NA>
3 -87.52503 30.37249     1     3 alabama      <NA>
4 -87.53076 30.33239     1     4 alabama      <NA>
5 -87.57087 30.32665     1     5 alabama      <NA>
6 -87.58806 30.32665     1     6 alabama      <NA>

Codehead(elections_by_state) 

   state_name state_abbr repub_pct_20 repub_20_categories
1     alabama         AL        62.03               60-64
2    arkansas         AR        62.40               60-64
3     arizona         AZ        49.06               45-49
4  california         CA        34.33               30-34
5    colorado         CO        41.90               40-44
6 connecticut         CT        39.21               35-39


Now map repub_pct_20 by state.

Code# Note where the dataset, elections_by_state, is used
# Note where the background map, states_map, is used
ggplot(elections_by_state, aes(map_id = state_name, fill = repub_pct_20)) +
  geom_map(map = states_map) +
  expand_limits(x = states_map$long, y = states_map$lat) +
  theme_map() 








Code# Make it nicer!
ggplot(elections_by_state, aes(map_id = state_name, fill = repub_pct_20)) +
  geom_map(map = states_map) +
  expand_limits(x = states_map$long, y = states_map$lat) +
  theme_map() + 
  scale_fill_gradientn(name = "% Republican", colors = c("blue", "purple", "red"), values = scales::rescale(seq(0, 100, by = 5)))







It’s not easy to get fine control over the color scale for the quantitative repub_pct_20 variable. Instead, let’s plot the discretized version, repub_20_categories:

Codeggplot(elections_by_state, aes(map_id = state_name, fill = repub_20_categories)) +
  geom_map(map = states_map) +
  expand_limits(x = states_map$long, y = states_map$lat) +
  theme_map()








Code# Load package needed for refining color palette
library(RColorBrewer)

# Now fix the colors
ggplot(elections_by_state, aes(map_id = state_name, fill = repub_20_categories)) +
  geom_map(map = states_map) +
  expand_limits(x = states_map$long, y = states_map$lat) +
  theme_map() + 
  scale_fill_manual(values = rev(brewer.pal(8, "RdBu")), name = "% Republican")







✏️ Add Starbucks Layer
We can add other layers, like points, on top of a choropleth map. Add a Starbucks layer! Do you notice any relationship between Starbucks and elections? Or are we just doing things at this point? ;)

Code# Get only the starbucks data from the US
starbucks_us <- starbucks |> 
  filter(Country == "US")

# Map it
ggplot(elections_by_state, aes(map_id = state_name, fill = repub_20_categories)) +
  geom_map(map = states_map) +
  geom_point(
    data = starbucks_us,
    aes(x = Longitude, y = Latitude),
    size = 0.05,
    alpha = 0.2,
    inherit.aes = FALSE
  ) +
  expand_limits(x = states_map$long, y = states_map$lat) +
  theme_map() + 
  scale_fill_manual(values = rev(brewer.pal(8, "RdBu")), name = "% Republican")







Details (if you’re curious)


map_id is a required aesthetic for geom_map().

It specifies which variable in our dataset indicates the region (here state_name).
It connects this variable (state_name) to the region variable in our mapping background (states_map). These variables must have the same possible outcomes in order to be matched up (alabama, alaska, arizona,…).



expand_limits() assures that the map covers the entire area it’s supposed to, by pulling longitudes and latitudes from the states_map.
✏️ Name Choropleth Geom
We used geom_sf() for point maps. What geom do we use for choropleth maps?
✏️ Map Counties with Choropleth
Let’s map the 2020 Republican support in each county.
We again need two pieces of information.

Data on elections in each county, which we already have: elections_by_county.
A background map of county boundaries in the US, stored in the county_map dataset in the socviz package:


Code# Get the latitude and longitude coordinates of county boundaries
library(socviz)
data(county_map) 

# Check it out
head(county_map)

2 1235324 -1274008     2 FALSE     1 0500000US01001.1 01001

4 1244129 -1267515     4 FALSE     1 0500000US01001.1 01001
5 1272010 -1262889     5 FALSE     1 0500000US01001.1 01001
6 1276797 -1295514     6 FALSE     1 0500000US01001.1 01001


Important detail: We officially have a headache. Our county_map refers to each county by a 5-number id. Our elections_by_counties data refers to each county by a county_fips code, which is mostly the same as id, BUT drops any 0’s at the beginning of the code.

  state_name state_abbr    county_name county_fips repub_pct_20 median_age
1    Alabama         AL Autauga County        1001        71.44       37.5
2    Alabama         AL Baldwin County        1003        76.17       41.5
3    Alabama         AL Barbour County        1005        53.45       38.3

5    Alabama         AL  Blount County        1009        89.57       39.6

  median_rent repub_20_categories

This just means that we have to wrangle the data so that it can communicate with the background map.

Code# Add 0's at the beginning of any fips_code that's fewer than 5 numbers long
# Don't worry about the syntax
elections_by_counties <- elections_by_counties |> 
  mutate(county_fips = as.character(county_fips)) |> 
  mutate(county_fips = 
           ifelse(nchar(county_fips) == 4, paste0("0", county_fips), county_fips))


Now map Republican support by county. Let’s go straight to the discretized repub_20_categories variable, and a good color scale.

Codeggplot(elections_by_counties, aes(map_id = county_fips, fill = repub_20_categories)) +
  geom_map(map = county_map) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = rev(brewer.pal(10, "RdBu")), name = "% Republican") +
  expand_limits(x = county_map$long, y = county_map$lat) +
  theme_map() +
  theme(legend.position = "right") + 
  coord_equal()







✏️ Map Median Rent
Construct a county-level map of median_rent.

Codeggplot(elections_by_counties, aes(map_id = county_fips, fill = median_rent)) +
  geom_map(map = county_map) +
  expand_limits(x = county_map$long, y = county_map$lat) +
  theme_map() +
  theme(legend.position = "right") +
  coord_equal() +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "Median Rent")







✏️ Map Median Age
Construct a county-level map of median_age.

Codeggplot(elections_by_counties, aes(map_id = county_fips, fill = median_age)) +
  geom_map(map = county_map) +
  expand_limits(x = county_map$long, y = county_map$lat) +
  theme_map() +
  theme(legend.position = "right") +
  coord_equal() +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "Median Age")







✏️ Build Choropleth with Leaflet
Though ggplot() is often better for this purpose, we can also make choropleth maps with leaflet(). If you’re curious, check out the leaflet documentation:
https://rstudio.github.io/leaflet/choropleths.html

title: Multivariate Viz
text:
SAT & Spending
Though far from a perfect assessment of academic preparedness, SAT scores have historically been used as one measurement of a state’s education system. The education dataset contains various education variables for each state:
Code# Load packages
library(tidyverse)

# Import and check out data
education <- read.csv("https://mac-stat.github.io/data/sat.csv")
head(education)

       State expend ratio salary frac verbal math  sat  fracCat
1    Alabama  4.405  17.2 31.144    8    491  538 1029   (0,15]
2     Alaska  8.963  17.6 47.951   47    445  489  934 (45,100]
3    Arizona  4.778  19.3 32.175   27    448  496  944  (15,45]
4   Arkansas  4.459  17.1 28.934    6    482  523 1005   (0,15]
5 California  4.992  24.0 41.078   45    417  485  902  (15,45]
6   Colorado  5.443  18.4 34.571   29    462  518  980  (15,45]
A codebook is provided by Danny Kaplan who also made these data accessible:

title: Multivariate Viz
text:
✏️ Plot SAT Scores
Construct a plot of how the average sat scores vary across states (HINT: you need to use the sat variable only).

Codeggplot(education, aes(x = sat)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 25, color = "white") +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Average SAT Scores Across States",
    x = "Average SAT score",
    y = "Number of states"
  )







✏️ Summarize SAT Distribution
Summarize your observations from the plot. Comment on the basics: range, typical outcomes, shape. (Any theories about what might explain this non-normal shape?)
The average state SAT scores range from roughly the mid-800s to a little above 1100. Rather than forming one symmetric, bell-shaped distribution, the scores appear to form two broad groups: one group is concentrated around about 880–950 and another around about 1000–1100. Therefore, a single “typical” center does not describe the distribution especially well, although many states fall near the 900s or just above 1000. The non-normal, roughly bimodal shape is likely related to differences in SAT participation among states. In states where only a small fraction of students take the SAT, the test-takers tend to be a more selective group of college-bound students, which can produce higher state averages.
✏️ Plot SAT vs Spending
The first question we’d like to answer is: Can the variability in sat scores from state to state be partially explained by how much a state spends on education, specifically its per pupil spending (expend) and typical teacher salary?

Code# Construct a plot of sat vs expend
# Include a "best fit linear regression model" (HINT: method = "lm")
ggplot(education, aes(x = expend, y = sat)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  labs(
    title = "SAT Score vs. Per-Pupil Expenditure",
    x = "Per-pupil expenditure",
    y = "Average SAT score"
  )







✏️ Plot SAT vs Salary

Code# Construct a plot of sat vs salary
# Include a "best fit linear regression model" (HINT: method = "lm")
ggplot(education, aes(x = salary, y = sat)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  labs(
    title = "SAT Score vs. Teacher Salary",
    x = "Typical teacher salary",
    y = "Average SAT score"
  )







✏️ Describe Spending Trends
What are the relationship trends between SAT scores and spending? Is there anything that surprises you?
Both plots show an overall negative association: states with higher per-pupil expenditures and higher teacher salaries tend to have lower average SAT scores. This is surprising because I would normally expect greater educational spending to be associated with equal or better academic outcomes. However, these plots only show the overall association and do not account for other variables, especially the percentage of students in each state who take the SAT.

title: Multivariate Viz
text:
Trivariate Viz
✏️ Combine Spending & Salaries
Construct one visualization of the relationship of sat with salary and expend. HINT: Start with just 2 variables and tweak that code to add the third variable. Try out a few things!

Codeggplot(education, aes(x = salary, y = sat, color = expend)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  labs(
    title = "SAT Scores, Teacher Salary, and Per-Pupil Spending",
    x = "Typical teacher salary",
    y = "Average SAT score",
    color = "Expenditure"
  )







This graph uses position for salary and sat and color for expend, allowing all three quantitative variables to be viewed at the same time.
✏️ Discretize Scale
It can be tough to distinguish color scales and size scales for quantitative variables. Another option is to discretize a quantitative variable, or basically cut it up into categories.
Construct the plot below. Check out the code and think about what’s happening here. What happens if you change “2” to “3”?

Codeggplot(education, aes(y = sat, x = salary, color = cut(expend, 2))) + 
  geom_point() + 
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE, method = "lm")







✏️ Describe Trivariate Relationship
Describe the trivariate relationship between sat, salary, and expend.
Teacher salary and per-pupil expenditure tend to increase together, so states with higher salaries often also have higher spending. Looking at SAT scores at the same time, the higher-spending/higher-salary states tend to have lower average SAT scores in the overall data. After discretizing expend, the separate expenditure groups make it easier to see that the apparent relationship is more complicated than a single overall line. This suggests that another variable may be influencing both the spending pattern and the observed SAT averages.
Changing cut(expend, 2) to cut(expend, 3) divides expenditure into three groups instead of two. That produces three colors and three separate fitted regression lines, giving a more detailed comparison across low-, medium-, and high-spending states.

title: Multivariate Viz
text:
Simpson’s Paradox
It’s strange that SAT scores seem to decrease with spending. But we’re leaving out an important variable from our analysis: the fraction of a state’s students that actually take the SAT. The fracCat variable indicates this fraction: low (under 15% take the SAT), medium (15-45% take the SAT), and high (at least 45% take the SAT).
✏️ Plot SAT Participation
Build a univariate viz of fracCat to better understand how many states fall into each category.

Codeggplot(education, aes(x = fracCat)) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(
    title = "Number of States by SAT Participation Category",
    x = "SAT participation category",
    y = "Number of states"
  )







✏️ Relate SAT to Participation
Build 2 bivariate visualizations that demonstrate the relationship between sat and fracCat. What story does your graphic tell and why does this make contextual sense?

Code# Visualization 1: side-by-side boxplots
ggplot(education, aes(x = fracCat, y = sat)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(
    title = "SAT Scores by Participation Category",
    x = "SAT participation category",
    y = "Average SAT score"
  )






Code# Visualization 2: jittered points
ggplot(education, aes(x = fracCat, y = sat)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, height = 0) +
  labs(
    title = "State SAT Scores by Participation Category",
    x = "SAT participation category",
    y = "Average SAT score"
  )







The graphics show a very strong relationship between SAT participation and average SAT score. States in the low participation category generally have the highest SAT averages, while states in the high participation category generally have the lowest averages. This makes contextual sense because when only a small percentage of students take the SAT, those students are likely to be a more self-selected, college-bound group. When participation is high, the test-taking group represents a much broader range of students, so the state average tends to be lower.
✏️ Add Participation to Spending Plot
Make a trivariate visualization that demonstrates the relationship of sat with expend AND fracCat. Highlight the differences in fracCat groups through color AND unique trend lines. What story does your graphic tell?
Does it still seem that SAT scores decrease as spending increases?

Codeggplot(education, aes(x = expend, y = sat, color = fracCat)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  labs(
    title = "SAT Score vs. Spending, Grouped by SAT Participation",
    x = "Per-pupil expenditure",
    y = "Average SAT score",
    color = "SAT participation"
  )







Once the states are separated by fracCat, the relationship changes. Within the participation groups, the fitted lines are generally flat to positive rather than showing the strong negative relationship seen in the overall plot. Therefore, it no longer makes sense to conclude that higher spending causes lower SAT scores. Much of the original negative trend was created by differences in SAT participation across states.
✏️ Explain Simpson’s Paradox
Putting all of this together, explain this example of Simpson’s Paradox. That is, why did it appear that SAT scores decrease as spending increases even though the opposite is true?
This is an example of Simpson’s Paradox because the direction of the relationship changes after accounting for a third variable. When all states are combined, higher educational spending appears to be associated with lower SAT scores. However, states differ greatly in the fraction of students who take the SAT. High-participation states tend to have lower SAT averages because they include a broader range of students, and many of these states also spend more on education. Low-participation states tend to have higher SAT averages because their test-takers are a more selective group, and many of those states spend less. Participation therefore confounds the overall relationship. Once we compare states within similar participation categories, the negative spending–SAT relationship largely disappears and becomes flat or positive. In other words, the pooled data give a misleading trend because they combine groups with very different SAT participation rates.

title: Multivariate Viz
text:
Heat Maps & Star Plots (Optional)
As usual, we’ve only just scratched the surface! There are lots of other data viz techniques for exploring multivariate relationships. Let’s start with a heat map.
✏️ Build Heat Maps
Run the chunks below. Check out the code, but don’t worry about every little detail! NOTES:

This is not part of the ggplot() grammar, making it a bit complicated.
If you’re curious about what a line in the plot does, comment it out (#) and check out what happens!
In the plot, for each state (row), each variable (column) is scaled to indicate whether the state has a relative high value (yellow), a relatively low value (purple), or something in between (blues/greens).
You can also play with the color scheme. Type ?cm.colors in the console to learn about various options.
We’ll improve the plot later, so don’t spend too much time trying to learn something from this plot.


Code# Remove the "State" column and use it to label the rows
# Then scale the variables
plot_data <- education |> 
  column_to_rownames("State") |> 
  data.matrix() |> 
  scale()

# Load the gplots package needed for heatmaps
library(gplots)

# Construct heatmap 1
heatmap.2(plot_data,
  dendrogram = "none",
  Rowv = NA, 
  scale = "column",
  keysize = 0.7, 
  density.info = "none",
  col = hcl.colors(256), 
  margins = c(10, 20),
  colsep = c(1:7), rowsep = (1:50), sepwidth = c(0.05, 0.05),
  sepcolor = "white", trace = "none"
)



Code# Construct heatmap 2
heatmap.2(plot_data,
  dendrogram = "none",
  Rowv = TRUE,             ### WE CHANGED THIS FROM NA TO TRUE
  scale = "column",
  keysize = 0.7, 
  density.info = "none",
  col = hcl.colors(256), 
  margins = c(10, 20),
  colsep = c(1:7), rowsep = (1:50), sepwidth = c(0.05, 0.05),
  sepcolor = "white", trace = "none"
)



Code# Construct heatmap 3
heatmap.2(plot_data,
  dendrogram = "row",       ### WE CHANGED THIS FROM "none" TO "row"
  Rowv = TRUE,            
  scale = "column",
  keysize = 0.7, 
  density.info = "none",
  col = hcl.colors(256), 
  margins = c(10, 20),
  colsep = c(1:7), rowsep = (1:50), sepwidth = c(0.05, 0.05),
  sepcolor = "white", trace = "none"
)


✏️ Interpret Heat Maps
In the final two plots, the states (rows) are rearranged by similarity with respect to these education metrics. The final plot includes a dendrogram which further indicates clusters of similar states. In short, states that have a shorter path to connection are more similar than others.
Putting this all together, what insight do you gain about the education trends across U.S. states? Which states are similar? In what ways are they similar? Are there any outliers with respect to 1 or more of the education metrics?
The heat maps show that states can be grouped into clusters with similar education profiles. Several Upper Midwest and Plains states, such as Minnesota, Wisconsin, Iowa, North Dakota, and South Dakota, are similar because they tend to have relatively high SAT scores and low SAT participation. In contrast, many Northeastern states, including Connecticut, Massachusetts, New Jersey, New York, Pennsylvania, and Rhode Island, tend to have higher spending and teacher salaries, higher SAT participation, and lower average SAT scores. These lower averages should not automatically be interpreted as worse education because participation differs greatly between the groups.
There are also some states that stand out on individual variables. Utah stands out for relatively low educational expenditure and a high student-teacher ratio while still having a high SAT average and very low SAT participation. New Jersey and New York stand out for especially high spending, while states such as North Dakota, Iowa, Minnesota, and Wisconsin stand out for high SAT averages. Overall, the clustering reinforces the idea that SAT score patterns are closely connected to participation and to broader regional education patterns.
✏️ Build Star Plot
Like heat maps, star plots indicate the relative scale of each variable for each state. Thus, we can use star maps to identify similar groups of states, and unusual states!
Construct and check out the star plot below. Note that each state has a “pie”, with each segment corresponding to a different variable. The larger a segment, the larger that variable’s value is in that state. For example:

Check out Minnesota. How does Minnesota’s education metrics compare to those in other states? What metrics are relatively high? Relatively low?
What states appear to be similar? Do these observations agree with those that you gained from the heat map?

Minnesota has a relatively high SAT score but a relatively low SAT participation rate. Its spending and teacher salary are closer to the middle of the states rather than being among the very highest. Minnesota looks similar to other Upper Midwest and Plains states such as Wisconsin, Iowa, and the Dakotas, which also combine relatively high SAT averages with low participation. This agrees with the grouping seen in the heat map. Northeastern states form a different pattern, with larger spending/salary segments and generally higher participation.

Codestars(plot_data,
  flip.labels = FALSE,
  key.loc = c(10, 1.5),
  cex = 1, 
  draw.segments = TRUE
)


✏️ Map Star Plots
Finally, let’s plot the state stars by geographic location! What new insight do you gain here?!
Placing the stars geographically makes the regional clustering much easier to see. Nearby states often have similar education profiles. Upper Midwest and Great Plains states tend to share the combination of low SAT participation and high SAT averages, while many Northeastern states show higher spending, higher teacher salaries, and higher SAT participation. This suggests that education metrics are not randomly distributed across the country; they reflect regional similarities in school systems and, especially, differences in which college entrance exam students typically take.

Codestars(plot_data,
  flip.labels = FALSE,
  locations = data.matrix(as.data.frame(state.center)),  # added external data to arrange by geo location
  key.loc = c(-110, 28),
  cex = 1, 
  draw.segments = TRUE
)
